articles.title: Make it yours

body.support:
You will read websites and reports for school and work. Using what you read is fine. **Copying it and saying it's yours is not.** That's **plagiarism**.

Copying a website, a friend or an AI tool counts. Changing a few words doesn't fix it.

There are three honest moves:

1. **Notes.** Write key words, not whole sentences.
2. **Paraphrase.** Read it. Cover it. Say it your way. Write it down.
3. **Summarise.** Give the main idea in a few words.

Using someone's exact words? Put them in **quotation marks**. And say where it came from: *“According to …”*
body.core:
You'll read websites, reports and textbooks for assignments, at TAFE and at work. Using what you read is fine — **copying it and pretending it's yours is not**. That's **plagiarism**.

Plagiarism includes copying a website, a friend's work or text from an AI tool and handing it in as your own. Changing a few words doesn't fix it. In VCE, work that can't be shown to be yours is treated as a **breach of the rules**. At work, it can cost you your job.

There are three honest moves:

1. **Notes.** Write **key words**, not whole sentences. Notes help you remember without copying.
2. **Paraphrase.** Read it, cover it, say it out loud in your own way, then write it down. Check you kept the meaning.
3. **Summarise.** Give just the **main idea** in fewer words. Ask: what's the one thing this is saying?

If you use someone's exact words, put them in **quotation marks**. And always **acknowledge** your source: *“According to the Fair Work Ombudsman, …”*
body.extend:
You'll read websites, reports and textbooks for assignments, at TAFE and at work. Using what you read is expected — **presenting it as your own is plagiarism**.

Plagiarism includes copying a website, a friend's work or AI-generated text, and “patchwriting” — swapping a few words but keeping someone else's sentences. In VCE, VCAA's rules require that all unacknowledged work you submit is your own; work that can't be authenticated is treated as a **breach of rules**. In workplaces, plagiarism can end careers.

The VCAA rules also say what *is* acceptable: using ideas from other sources that you've **transformed** and used in a new context. That's what these moves do:

1. **Notes.** Key words, not sentences, so you're not tempted to copy.
2. **Paraphrase.** Read, cover, say it your way, write, then check the meaning.
3. **Summarise.** Reduce a text to its main idea and purpose.

Use **quotation marks** for exact words, and **acknowledge** every source. Images and music are protected by **copyright** too: credit the creator and check you're allowed to use them.

caseStudies.title: The speech that copied

body.support:
In 2016, Melania Trump gave a big speech in the United States. People noticed some parts were almost the **same as a speech by Michelle Obama** from 2008.

A speechwriter said it was her mistake. She had copied parts without checking. She said sorry and **offered to quit her job**.

Everyone talked about the copying, not the speech.
body.core:
In July 2016, Melania Trump gave a big speech in the United States. Within hours, people noticed something. Some parts were almost the **same as a speech Michelle Obama gave in 2008**.

Two days later, a speechwriter called Meredith McIver said it was her mistake. Melania had read her parts of Michelle Obama's speech as examples. McIver wrote them into the draft. She didn't check them. She said sorry and **offered to quit her job**.

It became one of the biggest stories of the week. But it was about the copying, not the speech.

source.name: PBS NewsHour — “Trump speechwriter apologizes for Melania Trump's speech” (July 2016)

caseStudies.title: VCAA's rules for your own work

body.support:
The **VCAA** runs the VCE, including VCE VM. Its rules say:

- the work you hand in must be **your own**
- you must **say where your information came from**
- you can't get too much help

Ideas in **your own words** are OK. **Copying** is not.

If the school can't tell the work is yours, you have **broken the rules**.
body.core:
The **VCAA** runs the VCE. That includes VCE VM. It has rules about work you hand in for school. Here are the main ones.

- The work you hand in must be **your own**. The rule says: “all unacknowledged work submitted is their own”.
- You must **say where your information came from**. That includes texts and websites.
- You can't get **too much help** from other people. That includes your teacher.

So what is OK? You can use ideas from other places. But you must change them into your own work. What is not OK? Copying someone else's work. Copying a sample answer.

What if the school can't tell that the work is yours? Then it counts as **breaking the rules**.
body.extend:
The **VCAA** runs the VCE, including VCE VM. Its rules for school-based work include these:

- “a student must make sure that all unacknowledged work submitted is their own”
- a student must **acknowledge all resources used**, such as texts and websites
- a student must not get **undue assistance**. That means too much help, even from a teacher.

The rules say some help is fine. You can use ideas from other sources if you have **transformed** them and used them in a new way. Copying someone's work or a sample answer is not fine.

If any part of the work can't be shown to be yours, it is treated as a **breach of rules**.

source.name: VCAA Administrative Handbook — authentication rules for school-based assessment

teacher.overview: Students learn what plagiarism is and why it matters, then practise the three honest moves: key-word **notes**, **paraphrasing** and **summarising**, plus acknowledging sources. The texts are a real plagiarism case (the 2016 convention speech) and VCAA's own authentication rules, which students annotate, summarise and acknowledge.
prep: Have your school's VCE/VCE VM authentication policy ready to compare with the VCAA rules.
Decide your school's position on AI tools so you can answer questions consistently.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — What counts as copying?
steps: **Hook (5 min):** “Copy, paste, submit” — what happens when your teacher asks you to explain it?
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** plagiarism; model notes vs copying with a short article.
**Watch (5 min):** explainer.
**Read (15 min):** Make it yours + questions.
**Exit:** one OK and one not-OK use of a source.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Paraphrase it
steps: **Sort (10 min):** OK or not OK?
**Model (10 min):** read, cover, say, write — think aloud.
**Independent (20 min):** Paraphrase it table.
**Share (10 min):** compare paraphrases; did any change the meaning?

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Real cases, real rules
steps: **Case study (15 min):** the speech that copied.
**Annotate (20 min):** VCAA's rules: who, for whom, purpose; key-word notes.
**Discuss (15 min):** compare with the school policy.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Say it your way
steps: **Model (10 min):** summarise a short text in 30 words, then acknowledge it.
**Write (25 min):** final mission; fast finishers: source note and copyright question.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

keyPoints: Plagiarism = presenting others' words or ideas as your own (including AI text and patchwriting).
Notes = key words; paraphrase = read, cover, say, write, check; summary = main idea, fewer words.

VCAA: all unacknowledged work must be your own; work that can't be authenticated is a breach of rules.

**OK or not OK?** Copy a paragraph — Not OK. Explain in own words from three sites — OK if credited. Short quote in marks — OK if credited. Friend writes intro — Not OK. Teacher's general advice — OK. Same essay twice — Not OK.

**Speech case:** passages matched Michelle Obama's 2008 speech; the speechwriter wrote them in from examples read aloud, apologised and offered to resign.

**VCAA rules (purpose/audience):** written by the VCAA for schools and students, to make sure assessed work is genuinely the student's own.
